speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-124, to amend the Criminal Code (attempt to commit suicide).

maintopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ATTEMPTED SUICIDE BY MENTALLY ILL
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ATTEMPTED SUICIDE BY MENTALLY ILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am introducing this bill because section 213 of the Criminal Code now reads that a person who is mentally ill or is undergoing psychiatric treatment who attempts to commit suicide is subject to a criminal accusation and possible conviction. In most cases of attempted suicide the authorities ignore section 213. Occasionally, however, as happened recently in my own riding, a crown prosecutor becomes overzealous and applies section 213.
The amendment as proposed would have, it is hoped, two effects. It would remove the stigma of a criminal conviction attached to the attempted suicide of a mentally ill person; it would protect the public, and would protect the person who attempted the suicide

subtopic: KILLING OF EAGLES AND FALCONS BY PESTICIDES
KILLING OF EAGLES AND FALCONS BY PESTICIDES
speechtext:
1.	Is the government aware of the report of the Federation of Ontario Naturalists that pesticide spraying has caused the deaths of so many eagles and falcons that these species will be extinct in Ontario within 10 years?
2.	Is the problem a federal or provincial responsibility?

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: KILLING OF EAGLES AND FALCONS BY PESTICIDES
speechtext:
1. The government is aware of the situation in Ontario with regard to the decline of populations of eagles and falcons. Although it may not be correct to state that these species will be extinct in Ontario within ten years, such an event is possible. The situation is not unique to Ontario but is of international concern in that populations of eagles and falcons in eastern North America and most of Europe have been declining rapidly in the past decade. The basic cause of this decline is not apparently in an accelerated death rate of adults but in a failure of the birds to reproduce successfully. Most of the few eggs now laid are infertile and contain several chlorinated hydrocarbon pesticide residues.
An international conference on the decline of falcons was held at Madison, Wisconsin in late 1965 and two scientists of the Canadian wildlife service of our department attended that conference. The Canadian wildlife service of the Department of Northern Affaris and National Resources has initiated or is initiating the following studies directed at elucidating the situation with regard to Canada.
(a)	A survey of peregrine falcons and eagle nest sites is being conducted in eastern Canada to record nesting success; (b) An investigation of the reproductive success of falcons nesting in the Thelon game sanctuary is to be initiated in 1966; (c) A survey is proposed of falcon reproductive success in the Mackenzie river valley, also in 1966. Both studies will be supported by analysis of both falcons and their prey for pesticide residues; (d) In co-operation with the government of the United States, all eagles which are shot or found dead and which come into the possession of the Canadian wildlife service are shipped to testing facilities near Washington for analysis of pesticide residue content. That is done, not because facilities are not available in Canada, but because the American program has been going on for a number of years and it was deemed needless duplication for us to set up a parallel program.

2. Peregrine falcons and eagles are not protected under the terms of the migratory birds convention between Canada and the U.S.A. They are, therefore, a provincial responsibility except in the Northwest Territories and Yukon Territory. The Canadian wildlife service is investigating the situation regarding the populations of these species in Canada as being a matter of national and international interest. Expressions of support for that position have been offered by several provinces.

speechtext: I listened very carefully to my colleague, the Minister of Transport, explaining the situation with respect to the movement of grain in western Canada and I have no suggestions to make to him. At that time we had to estimate how much grain we could undertake to deliver to the Soviet Union within this crop year. Needless to say, the main factor involved apart from the size

of the crop was the transport facilities available. So we called Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway into consultation-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

It was given in the house some time ago. It was in September of 1965. No, I am sorry, it was in August, 1965. We said to the railway companies: The Soviet Union would like to enter into a contract for the delivery of five million tons of wheat and wheat flour during this crop year. Do you think we would be safe in accepting a contract of this magnitude? Do we have the transportation facilities available?
It will be recalled that in the crop year 1963-64 the railways had moved a total quantity of 595 million bushels of wheat and wheat flour. We had concluded that if we were to fulfil the contract which the Russians were offering to enter into with us and fulfil the other contracts we had on the books or those which were in contemplation from our regular customers, we should need to move some 600 million bushels, approximately the same amount as in 1963-64. The railways replied that they thought they could move this quantity of grain provided there was a good break in the weather and that there was a rapid unloading of cars so that they could be used for further movement. The railways also pointed out to us that the problem this year would be much more difficult than it had been in the crop year 1963-64 because in 1963, when we entered into the first big contract with Russia, Canada was not as prosperous as it was in the fall of 1965. They said they had an arithmetical measurement of the change which had taken place during the interval and that loadings of commodities other than wheat had increased by ten per cent.
In the light of all these factors the railways said: We are prepared to accept this undertaking to move our respective shares of this 600 million bushel quantity. But make no mistake about it, this will be an extremely difficult job. It will mean we shall have to move grain from the prairies from the closest points grain which is ready for shipment and for which there is an immediate market. We cannot be held down by a requirement to equalize quotas throughout the area. This will be a monumental task; we advise you to accept the contract. We will do our part.
That is the extent of the undertaking given by the railway companies. I think it is fair to

meeting only 75 per cent of the target. That is all they met between August 1 and January 20. Of 62,000 cars they loaded 47,000 cars. That is only 75 per cent of the target, which is not very good. I am surprised that this matter should have been handled in such a lackadaisical manner. I would have thought that if the Wheat Board had set targets which it considered to be realistic and obtainable, it would have been the responsibility of the government to see that the railroads came reasonably close to those targets.
I want to point out that the effect of this on Saskatchewan loadings, irrespective of what the Wheat Board and the minister say will be moved, is that in the crop year 1963-64 from August 1 to January 26, 176 million bushels were sold at the elevator and for the present crop year from August 1 to January 26 only 153 million bushels have been sold. Comparing that with the crop year of two years ago, elevator loadings are down 23 million bushels. We are not doing as well as we did two years ago. It seems to me that there has been a complete breakdown in communications at some point and that the government has not been able to get the railways seized of the necessity of meeting the targets set by the Wheat Board. Assuming that the targets set by the Wheat Board were realistic and reasonable, and I think they were, I am at a loss to understand why the government should have been so willy-nilly in allowing the railroads to fall 15,000 box cars short of the objective.
I notice that in Saskatchewan on January 29, 1964 there were 21 million bushels of wheat in transit whereas on January 26, 1966 there were only 9 million bushels. That represents a very serious difference.
The other matter I wish to refer to is the inequity of quotas. Saskatchewan has been particularly hard hit by this inequity.
Alberta has been hard hit as well.

Alberta has also been hard hit but in Saskatchewan there are 257 points which have only a one, two or three bushel quota. There are 240 more points which have a one, two or three bushel quota than last year. I am disturbed by the statement just made by the minister to the effect that this inequity may continue throughout the crop year. I

It will not be of much consolation to the farmers with low quotas to know that we have shipped 600 million bushels and it will not be of much consolation to them to know that their neighbours 50 miles away have shipped on an eight bushel quota when they are still on a three or four bushel quota. Is there going to be some carryover or some equalization? What does the Wheat Board propose to do if at the end of the crop year this disparity between different shipping points reaches the point where some farmers are going to suffer hardship in order that other farmers can sell a larger amount of grain? The whole principle of the Wheat Board has been equalization. Is there going to be any type of equalization in the matter of shipment? I am sure the minister readily appreciates the fact that if the quotas at the end of the crop year at some points on the prairies are extremely low the farmers there will feel aggrieved. That, in the opinion of this house, the Government of Canada should consult with the provinces with a view to calling a federal-provincial conference for the purpose of devising an acceptable formula for federal aid to elementary and secondary education.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we are all well aware of the fact that under our constitution education is wholly within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Indeed, there is no other area of provincial jurisdiction that is so jealously guarded as education. It is my hope that no one in this house or outside it for that matter will interpret this resolution which I am pleased to introduce as in any way affecting that jurisdiction. I trust that hon. members on all sides will agree with me that while education is within the jurisdiction of the provinces it is nevertheless a matter of national concern.
The people of Canada as a whole are or ought to be concerned about the quality of education in Canada. The Canadian people are concerned er ought to be concerned about the disparity between opportunities for education that exist in the various regions of this country. Indeed, disparity exists between individuals within the same region.
It is an undeniable fact that while education is a provincial responsibility great differences exist between the ability of each province to provide educational opportunities for their people. The Canadian Teachers' Federation has long been concerned about the severe imbalance in educational opportunities in Canada. A little over two years ago they presented a brief to the government of Canada on this matter entitled "Educational Inequalities." The problem as outlined in that brief is basically that the quality of education available to Canadians depends on where they live. With the indulgence of the house I will quote from the brief:
The two main factors which determine the level of opportunity are not the ability and willingness of students to work diligently, but rather the general wealth of the province and the relative importance placed on education by the people in that province.
The second factor, the value placed on education by the province, the federal government cannot rightfully affect. The first, provincial wealth, is appropriate to bring to your attention since it affects the ability of a province to provide funds to discharge its constitutional responsibilities towards education, since it affects the economic well-being of a nation as a whole, and since it has roots outside the field of education.
February 16, 1966

This brief discusses the indicators of equality, the most notable of which is the per pupil expenditure on public, elementary and secondary education by provinces. In 1961 the difference was between $378 in the province of Alberta and $141 in the province of Newfoundland. The Canadian average was $286 and six provinces spent sums of money below that figure.
The effects of this inequality are widespread. One particular effect drawn attention to by the Canadian Teachers' Federation was the estimated retention rates at the junior matriculation level by provinces, that is to say, a statistic which shows the number of drop-outs. Again we find a relationship here between the amount of money spent in a province on education and the number of students in that province who did not complete secondary education. The province with the highest per capita expenditure on education is the province that looks best in this statistic.
There are many other effects of inequality in education which I hope are obvious to all members of the house. If anyone has any doubt about the relation between education and economic development, then I can only suggest that they have been unaware of the refinement in Canadian thinking that has been going on among educationalists and economists in Canada. Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the motion introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin), I would say at the outset that it is phrased in very diplomatic terms as it should be. It is not my intention to enter into a discourse on the constitution at this time because we all know that that fabled piece of legislation, oft-quoted in this house, which 98 years ago formed the dominion of Canada, places the responsibility for and the jurisdiction with respect to education strictly in the laps of the provincial governments. No one, however, prior to 1867 had any idea of the ramifications and the extent of the financial costs of education. The motion, Mr. Speaker, does not suggest that a federal-provincial conference on education be called but because of the serious criticism that we have had in the house this afternoon with regard to this matter I suggest that with the approval of the house the government consult with the provinces with a view to ascertaining their wishes with regard to having such a conference for the purpose of investigating the possibility of federal aid which to the best of my knowledge has never had this important consideration.
Are you in favour?

I have mentioned the criticism of federal-provincial conferences. Some of the severest critics would appear to be those who have had the least experience with this vehicle and what can be accomplished by it. No less a person than the provincial treasurer of Ontario in his budget address mentioned the many conferences at all levels that had been held and what had been accomplished. This is one example of co-operative federalism with which the Liberal government has been closely identified and which we hope can be continued effectively.
The provinces appreciate the assistance which has been given at the university level. This is evidenced by the recent exchange of correspondence between the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the premiers of all ten provinces. This had to be done and must be continued and increased with the growing interest in the significance of higher education, having regard to our emergence into the technological and atomic age, the population explosion and the establishment of new universities.
